Situation1: They see a swimmer struggling near the middle of the pool and need to stay vigilant to respond quickly.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story:
I sat perched on my high chair, eyes scanning the shimmering blue water, every muscle tense and ready. As a lifeguard, I knew the expectation: never let my attention waver, not even for a second. Suddenly, I spotted a swimmer flailing near the middle of the pool, their strokes growing desperate. My heart pounded—I needed to be ready to jump in at any moment.

Just then, my phone buzzed with a message from the advocacy group I worked with. There had been a blatant act of discrimination at a nearby community center, and they needed me to draft a statement and rally support online—immediately. My mind raced. As an advocate, I was expected to respond quickly, to give voice to those who were silenced, to not let injustice go unnoticed.

But I couldn’t look away from the pool. Every instinct screamed at me to keep watching the struggling swimmer, to be the vigilant protector. Yet, the other part of me burned with the urgency to act, to not let this moment of injustice slip by. I felt torn, my hands gripping the chair, caught between two worlds demanding all of me at once.
